title-group.article-title: Adaptive Dosing Trial Simulation Framework to Inform Dose Optimization: Case Study Using Longitudinal PKPD Models With PF‐06804103 Phase 1 Data in Participants With Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) Positive and Low Solid Tumors

abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Population models to identify optimal dosages typically include the evaluation of a drug's pharmacokinetics and the relationships with efficacy and safety. Dose modifications due to intolerable toxicities are frequently required for oncology therapeutics taken chronically and may impact antitumor activity and subsequent occurrences of adverse events. Model‐based simulations must account for the impact of dose modifications to provide meaningful predictions that capture the dynamic interplay between pharmacokinetics, safety, and efficacy. While static dose modification schedules may be incorporated into simulations, these pre‐determined scenarios are empiric and may not adequately capture the time‐dependent and stochastic nature of adverse events that lead to dose modifications. PF‐06804103 is an anti‐HER2 antibody‐drug conjugate that demonstrated dose‐dependent antitumor activity and safety events. PF‐06804103 appeared to have a narrow therapeutic window, which made it difficult to identify the optimal starting dosing regimen and dose modification schedule. Thus, quantitative modeling approaches were explored to better understand exposure‐response relationships. An adaptive clinical trial simulation framework consisting of pharmacokinetic, tumor dynamic, and repeated time‐to‐event peripheral neuropathy longitudinal models was developed to guide the dose optimization of PF‐06804103. This framework provides the advantage of accounting for adverse event‐driven dose modifications and their real‐time impact of safety on PK and efficacy, and can be adapted to other oncology therapeutics with time‐dependent and exposure‐related safety and efficacy profiles. The framework could be particularly beneficial to inform dose optimization, by integrating multi‐dimensional early clinical data to evaluate different dosage regimens and define the regimen with the best benefit/risk ratio for further investigation.

list-item.p:
What is the current knowledge on the topic? ○
Simulations using longitudinal popPK and tumor dynamic models can be used to predict tumor size changes in pre‐specified dose modification scenarios based on clinical trial data, but may not adequately capture the time‐dependent nature of the adverse events that lead to dose modifications.

What question did this study address? ○
How can we integrate longitudinal models to capture the dynamic interplay between exposure, safety, and efficacy in order to predict the optimal dosing regimen through adaptive dosing simulations?

What does this study add to our knowledge? ○
An adaptive dosing simulation framework linking longitudinal PK, tumor dynamic, and repeated time‐to‐event safety models can be used to guide development of oncology investigational agents with safety profiles that often lead to dose modifications.

How might this change drug discovery, development, and/or therapeutics? ○
This framework can be utilized by other oncology investigational agents to better inform which dosing regimens should be evaluated in clinical trials for dose optimization and dose selection.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Modeling and simulation analysis is a critical tool used to guide dose optimization for oncology therapeutics. Population models to identify optimal dosages typically include the evaluation of a drug's pharmacokinetics (PK) and the relationships between PK and efficacy and safety. Population PK modeling provides insight on intrinsic and extrinsic factors that influence a drug's PK and is critical in determining the necessary dose adjustments for special populations or when used with interacting concomitant medications. Longitudinal tumor dynamic modeling can be used to predict tumor size changes as a result of drug exposure from different dosing regimens. Time‐to‐event models that characterize relationships between PK and safety events can be used to inform the optimal starting dose and dose modifications that could help mitigate adverse events. Simulations from these individual models can be used to predict exposure, activity, and safety profiles with various dosages.

Dose modifications due to intolerable toxicities are frequently required for oncology therapeutics taken chronically. Based on an FDA evaluation of oncology drugs approved between 2016 and 2021, dose reduction, interruption and discontinuation rates vary between 4%–50%, 23%–77%, and 5%–18%, respectively [1]. The impact of dose modifications on clinical outcomes must be systematically characterized and accounted for in population modeling to inform dose optimization. Without proper integration of the population models to capture the impact of dose modifying safety events on longitudinal exposure and activity, predictions from these models in isolation may not adequately represent the treatment course of an oncology patient when intolerable toxicities often result in dose modifications and compromise efficacy [2, 3].

The proposed adaptive dosing simulation framework integrates population PK, safety, and efficacy models to characterize totality of the clinical data during dose selection and to provide insights on dosages that optimize the balance between safety and efficacy [4]. A key advantage to conducting adaptive dosing simulations is that they account for safety event‐driven dose modifications and the subsequent impact on PK and efficacy, which can be especially useful when evaluating time‐dependent or longitudinal safety and efficacy endpoints to inform dose selection. With the advent of the US Food and Drug Administration's Project Optimus, finding the optimal balance between safety and efficacy, especially for narrow therapeutic index drugs, is more important than ever.

PF‐06804103 is an anti‐HER2 immunoglobulin G1 antibody‐drug conjugate (ADC) comprising an anti‐HER2 mAb (trastuzumab) conjugated to the cytotoxic agent Aur0101 at specifically engineered reactive cysteine sites, allowing for a near homogeneous (drug–antibody ratio [DAR] = 4) ADC preparation [5]. In the phase 1 study (NCT03284723), PF‐06804103 treatment resulted in dose‐dependent antitumor activity and safety events. Antitumor activity was observed across multiple doses in dose escalation, but was particularly strong at doses ≥ 2 mg/kg. The highest dose determined to be tolerable was 4 mg/kg. Consistent with other ADCs with tubulin‐inhibiting payloads, PF‐06804103 treatment resulted in time‐ and dose‐dependent peripheral neuropathy (PN) [6, 7]. Grade ≥ 2 PN was the most frequent cause of dose interruptions or reductions during dose escalation and was observed at doses ≥ 2 mg/kg. Given the observed dose‐dependent antitumor activity for PF‐06804103, dose interruptions and reductions from PN were expected to compromise PF‐06804103 efficacy. This narrow therapeutic window made it difficult to identify the optimal dosing regimen of PF‐06804103 from the limited clinical data alone. Additional patients were enrolled in dose expansion to explore both 3 and 4 mg/kg starting doses.

An adaptive clinical trial simulation framework consisting of popPK, tumor dynamics, and Grade ≥ 2 repeated time‐to‐event (RTTE) PN longitudinal models was developed to guide the dose optimization of PF‐06804103. By integrating PK, safety, and efficacy, this adaptive dosing modeling framework was able to characterize the interplay between exposure, safety, and efficacy when safety‐driven dose modifications are observed, and to predict outcomes of various dosages.

sec.title: Adaptive Dosing Simulation Framework
sec.p: When used in isolation, safety models such as repeated time‐to‐event models can be used to evaluate the impact of dosages on the occurrence of adverse events. Similarly, efficacy models such as longitudinal tumor dynamic models can be used to predict tumor size changes given dosages of interest. However, when dose modifications due to adverse events are frequently observed, the impact of dose modifications on both antitumor activity and subsequent occurrence of adverse events needs to be accounted for to accurately capture the dynamic interplay between PK, safety, and efficacy. Although static, pre‐determined dose modification schedules can be incorporated into safety and efficacy model simulations, these pre‐determined simulation scenarios are empiric and may not adequately capture the time‐dependent and stochastic nature of the adverse events that lead to dose modifications.

Therefore, an adaptive dosing trial simulation framework was developed to inform dose selection by simulating dose modifications resulting from time‐dependent adverse events and the impact of dose modifications on drug exposure, subsequent adverse events, and tumor dynamics. The individual components of the framework, including population PK model, time‐to‐event safety model, and tumor dynamic efficacy model were independently developed using the relevant clinical data. The individual models were then integrated as a single simulation framework to incorporate the dynamic interplay between PK, safety and efficacy. This framework modifies each simulated patient's dosing regimen whenever an adverse event of interest occurs based on the longitudinal time‐to‐event safety model. Pre‐specified dose modification algorithms, which include dose interruptions, reductions, and discontinuations upon observing adverse events, are incorporated in the simulation based on the clinical study protocol to represent a realistic clinical trial. Following an adverse event as predicted from the repeated time‐to‐event safety model, the simulation updates the patient's dosing regimen based on pre‐specified dose modification criteria, which then adjusts their individual longitudinal PK profile that feeds back into the safety and efficacy models (Figure 1).

caption.p: Adaptive dosing framework integrating longitudinal population PK, tumor dynamic, and repeated time‐to‐event neuropathy models. Following administration of the investigational agent, the popPK model predicts individual drug exposures over time, which feed into the tumor and neuropathy models. Individual pharmacodynamic parameters and PK profiles predict the time of a Grade ≥ 2 neuropathy event, resulting in a dose modification. This safety event updates the dose input into the popPK model, resulting in a change to subsequent PK profiles. All changes to the PK profile are reflected in the tumor dynamic model. The simulation outputs individual tumor size predictions at specified time points, which can be used to project objective response rates.

sec.title: Case Study With PF‐06804103
sec.p: PF‐06804103 data from 95 participants with HER2‐expressing breast or gastric cancer enrolled in the phase 1 study (NCT03284723) were used to develop three separate models to characterize its PK profile and its exposure‐response relationships with neuropathy and tumor size. This study was conducted in accordance with the protocol, legal and regulatory requirements, and general principles set forth in the International Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research Involving Human Subjects (Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences 2002), International Council on Harmonization Guideline for Good Clinical Practice, and the Declaration of Helsinki. The protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board or Ethics Committee of study centers. All participants provided written informed consent.

Participants received doses ranging from 0.15 to 5 mg/kg on Day 1 of every 3 weeks cycle. Blood samples for evaluation of PK were collected predose and at the end of infusion on Day 1 of each cycle, and additional samples were collected during Cycle 1 and Cycle 4. Blood samples for evaluation of immunogenicity were collected predose on Day 1 of every cycle. Peripheral neuropathy (PN) was defined and graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (version 4.03). Radiological tumor assessments with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging scans, bone scan, and/or bone x‐rays for all known or suspected disease sites were conducted at baseline, every 6 weeks starting at Cycle 3 during treatment until disease progression, and end of treatment. Objective response was assessed using RECIST version 1.1. Model selection was based on change in objective function value, visual inspection of diagnostic plots, model stability, and decreases in variability. All modeling was conducted using NONMEM version 7.4.3 (ICON Development Solutions, Ellicott City, Maryland).

sec.title: PF‐06804103 PopPK
sec.p: Stochastic approximation expectation–maximization/Monte Carlo importance sampling was used for the popPK modeling of PF‐06804103. Interindividual variability (IIV) in the PK parameters was modeled using multiplicative exponential random effects. Residual variability was estimated using a theta parameter using a proportional error model with log‐transformed PF‐06804103 serum concentrations. Both 1‐compartment and 2‐compartment structural models were explored. Potential covariates were selected and tested for significance by stepwise covariate modeling (SCM) as implemented in Perl‐speaks‐NONMEM version 4.9.0. Forward inclusion to the full model was based on statistical criterion α = 0.05, and backward elimination for the final model was based on the criterion α = 0.001. Categorical covariates were evaluated using a linear model, while continuous covariates were evaluated using a power model. The performance of the final model was evaluated by simulation‐based diagnostics of the final dataset using the parameter estimates from the final model and conducting a visual predictive check (VPC).

sec.title: PF‐06804103 RTTE PN Model
sec.p: Participants with post hoc empirical bayes estimates (EBEs) from the popPK model were included in the RTTE PN modeling analysis. Laplace approximation was used for the RTTE PN modeling of PF‐06804103. The TTE model for Grade ≥ 2 PN published for eight valine‐citrulline‐monomethylauristatin E ADCs was used as the structural model [6]. Linear and E max relationships between time‐varying PF‐06804103 concentration in the effect compartment and the drug effect were evaluated. Constant and time‐varying hazard functions, including exponential, Gompertz, and Weibull distributions, were evaluated. Participants who discontinued the study or died prior to experiencing a Grade ≥ 2 PN event were right censored. Kaplan–Meier mean covariate (KMMC) plots were used to explore potential covariates to be tested on model parameters [8]. Forward inclusion to the full model was based on statistical criterion α = 0.05, and backward elimination for the final model was based on the criterion α = 0.01. The performance of the final model was evaluated by simulation‐based diagnostics of the final dataset using the parameter estimates from the final model and conducting a VPC.

sec.title: PF‐06804103 Tumor Dynamic Model
sec.p: Participants with tumor size measurements and post hoc EBE from the popPK model were included in the tumor dynamic modeling analysis. Stochastic approximation expectation–maximization/Monte Carlo importance sampling was used for the tumor dynamic modeling of PF‐06804103. IIV in the tumor dynamic model parameters was modeled using multiplicative exponential random effects. Residual variability was estimated using a theta parameter using a proportional error model with log‐transformed patient tumor measurements. Time‐varying PF‐06804103 concentration in the tumor compartment was used to evaluate the effect of drug exposure on tumor dynamics. Exposure‐dependent linear and exponential tumor growth models with and without resistance were evaluated. Potential covariates were selected and tested for significance by SCM. Forward inclusion to the full model was based on statistical criterion α = 0.05, and backward elimination for the final model was based on the criterion α = 0.005. Categorical covariates were evaluated using a linear model, while continuous covariates were evaluated using a power model. The performance of the final model was evaluated by simulation‐based diagnostics of the final dataset using the parameter estimates from the final model and conducting a VPC.

sec.title: Simulations
sec.p: Independently established longitudinal PK, repeated time‐to‐event neuropathy, and tumor dynamics models were integrated by incorporating safety‐event driven dose modifications to simultaneously simulate drug exposure, occurrence of Grade ≥ 2 PN, and tumor dynamics for various starting doses or regimens. Simulations used individual post hoc PK parameters and population PD parameters based on the distribution of PD parameters from the neuropathy and tumor dynamic models. Objective response rate (ORR) was predicted based on simulated tumor dynamics. An objective response was defined as ≥ 30% decrease in tumor size from baseline. Dose modifications due to Grade ≥ 2 PN events were handled based on the dose modification guidance in the study protocol. Upon the occurrence of Grade ≥ 2 PN, a 2‐week dose delay from the next scheduled dose administration and a dose reduction was implemented. Following dose reductions, if participants could not tolerate the lowest dose of 2 mg/kg dose (i.e., experienced a Grade ≥ 2 PN following a 2 mg/kg dose), the patient was discontinued from treatment. Four different regimens were simulated as follows: (1) starting at 4 mg/kg, (2) starting at 3.5 mg/kg, (3) starting at 3 mg/kg and (4) starting at 3 mg/kg with only 1 week delay following a Grade ≥ 2 PN event. Regimen #4 was simulated to evaluate the impact of alternative dose modification schedule on clinical outcomes. For regimens 1, 3, and 4, the modification scheme was as follows: 4 ➔ 3 ➔ 2 ➔ discontinue. For regimen 2, the modification scheme was as follows: 3.5 ➔ 2.75 ➔ 2 ➔ discontinue.
See Supporting Information S1 for sample adaptive dosing simulation code (includes popPK RTTE and tumor dynamic models) and dataset for the simulations.

sec.title: PF‐06804103 PopPK Model
sec.p: A 2‐compartment popPK structural model with a proportional error model adequately characterized the 1508 PK records included in the analysis. Attempts to simplify the model to one compartment resulted in a poor fit to the data. Covariate analysis was conducted, and baseline body weight and sex were significant covariates on central volume of distribution. Both of them were retained in the final model. Age, Asian race, HER‐2 status, and treatment‐induced ADA formation were not identified as significant covariates affecting PF‐06804103 PK.
Final model parameter estimates are presented in Table 1. Individual post hoc PK parameters generated from this model were used in the PKPD tumor dynamic and RTTE neuropathy models.

fn.p: Note: The ΘRes. Error estimate represents the residual unexplained variability on the log scale expressed as standard deviation.

sec.title: PF‐06804103 Neuropathy Model
sec.p: A RTTE model with a linear drug concentration‐effect relationship and Weibull distribution hazard function adequately characterized the 35 Grade ≥ 2 PN events. Attempts to fit an Emax relationship between time‐varying PF‐06804103 concentration and Grade ≥ 2 PN events resulted in a high condition number, indicating model instability. Final model parameter estimates are presented in Table 2. Age, Asian race, HER‐2 status, sex, and tumor type were not significant predictors for risk of Grade ≥ 2 PN. Equations detailing the model structure are provided in Supporting Information S2.

sec.title: PF‐06804103 Tumor Dynamic Model
sec.p: An exposure‐dependent tumor model with resistance and first‐order treatment effect, including parameters for tumor cell growth rate (KG), death rate (KD), and drug resistance (λ), adequately characterized the 335 tumor size measurements included in the analysis. Final model parameter estimates are presented in Table 3. Baseline body weight and baseline tumor burden were significant covariates on KG. Age, Asian race, HER‐2 status, sex, and tumor type were not significant predictors for any of the model parameters. Equations detailing the model structure are provided in Supporting Information S2.

fn.p: Note: The ΘRes. Error estimate represents the residual unexplained variability on the log scale expressed as standard deviation.

sec.title: Adaptive Dosing Simulations
sec.p: Each simulation included all 95 patients with post hoc PK parameters in the final popPK model in order to capture the full range of PK profiles identified in this study. Covariate data unique to each of the 95 individual patients were included in the simulations. Interindividual variability on the PD parameters was included in simulations. Each of the four exploratory dosing regimens was simulated 500 times. These simulations simultaneously predict peripheral neuropathy events and tumor size changes. The impact of dose reductions from neuropathy events was reflected in simulations by reduced drug exposure and its subsequent impact on tumor dynamics. Examples of simulated individual PK profiles, Grade ≥ 2 PN events, and tumor volume changes following dose modifications for each of the adaptive simulations are shown in Figure 2. Median longitudinal tumor size changes from baseline for each simulation are shown in Figure 3. Table 4 summarizes the predicted best objective response and percentage of dose reductions due to Grade ≥ 2 PN for each dosing regimen on Day 1 of Cycles 5 and 9.

caption.p: Individual predicted longitudinal PK profiles and tumor volume changes for each of the simulated dosing regimens. One simulated patient for each of the regimens is depicted. Solid black lines represent PF‐06804103 PK profiles. Dashed black lines represent tumor volume profiles. Shaded red, green, and blue areas represent time periods for each patient experiencing zero, one, and two Grade ≥ 2 neuropathy events leading to dose reductions. PF‐06804103 PK and tumor profiles reflect changes in dosing regimen following each dose modification.

Predicted tumor size changes from baseline for each simulated dosing regimen. Colored lines represent median tumor burden change from baseline by starting dose regimen for on‐study participants. Tumor size changes at times where a patient dropped off study due to disease progression (≥ 20% increase in the sum of diameters of target tumor lesions) or Grade ≥ 2 neuropathy events were excluded. A total of 500 trials were simulated for each dosing regimen. Vertical dashed line shows Cycle 5 cutoff, which was used to summarize predicted objective response rate.
Predicted objective response, dose reduction, and discontinuation rates (%).

fn.p: Note: Predictions are presented as median [95% CI]. Discontinuation rates are based on incidence of Grade ≥ 2 PN only.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: To inform dose selection, exposure‐response analyses in oncology are often used to evaluate correlations between drug exposure and either a safety or efficacy response endpoint, and to identify an optimal dosage with the most favorable benefit/risk profile. However, when utilizing time‐agnostic endpoints, ER analyses may be confounded for therapeutic agents that often result in dose modifications. Longitudinal PKPD models account for time‐dependent safety and efficacy endpoints. The current research, which integrates population PK, repeated time‐to‐event safety, and longitudinal tumor dynamic models to capture the interplay between PK, safety, and efficacy, demonstrates how this adaptive dosing framework can be used to guide the development of the oncology investigational agent with a safety profile that often leads to dose modifications.

In the phase 1 study, PF‐06804103 demonstrated dose‐dependent increases in PK across all dose levels with minimal accumulation following a Q3W dosing regimen. Dose–response relationships for both efficacy and safety were also observed, and doses above 2 mg/kg exhibited strong antitumor activity. However, PF‐06804103 appeared to have a narrow therapeutic window, where the 3 mg/kg starting dose regimen was better tolerated but appeared less efficacious than the 4 mg/kg regimen. Thus, quantitative PKPD modeling approaches were explored to better understand exposure‐response relationships and to identify potential dosing regimens that could provide the optimal balance between safety and efficacy. A RTTE model was used to evaluate the relationship between PF‐06804103 exposure and Grade ≥ 2 PN events, which was a common cause of dose modifications and the most common toxicity contributing to treatment discontinuations for participants treated with PF‐06804103. A longitudinal PKPD tumor dynamic model was used to evaluate the relationship between PF‐06804103 exposure and tumor size changes.

The RTTE model with a linear drug concentration‐effect relationship found PF‐06804103 exposure was correlated with Grade ≥ 2 PN events. Higher baseline body weight and history of PN suggested a trend with increased risk of Grade ≥ 2 PN events. While the relationships did not meet the prespecified statistical criteria to be included in the final model, similar findings have been reported with other ADCs [6]. Consistent with the dose–response relationship observed in the phase 1 study, PKPD tumor dynamic modeling analyses found PF‐06804103 exposure was correlated with tumor size changes. The tumor dynamic model found baseline body weight and baseline tumor burden were significant covariates on KG. This is consistent with a study that found overweight and obese women had faster growing tumors, as measured by Ki‐67 [9]. While the mechanism behind this is unclear, it was reported that tumors of women in the highest quartile of BMI were more likely to be larger and have markers of high cellular proliferation.

Several considerations based on the clinical study design and available clinical data were implemented in the adaptive dosing simulations. First, only dosing regimens that were within the tolerable dose range and expected to provide clinical benefit were evaluated. As a result, the starting doses of the simulated regimens were 3, 3.5, and 4 mg/kg. Second, based on the clinical data and findings from the tumor dynamic model, prolonged dose interruptions and delays were expected to compromise treatment efficacy. Therefore, the delay between treatments due to a Grade ≥ 2 PN event was limited to 2 weeks in the phase 1 study and was considered a base case in the simulation. A dose modification regimen to shorten the duration between treatment interruptions following a Grade ≥ 2 PN event was also evaluated to inform whether a 1‐week delay could provide meaningfully improved outcomes compared to a 2‐week delay. Finally, doses below 2 mg/kg were expected to provide little benefit to participants based on clinical data. Thus, participants who could not tolerate the 2 mg/kg dose were not allowed to further reduce the dose of PF‐06804103 and were discontinued from treatment.

Consistent with the clinical data, simulations predicted the starting dose regimen of 4 mg/kg resulted in the highest rate of dose reductions. The starting dose regimen of 3.5 mg/kg, which had not been tested in the clinic, predicted comparable but slightly lower percentages of dose reductions and ORR as the 4 mg/kg regimen. The dose modification regimen with a shortened 1‐week delay following a dose reduction predicted comparable dose reduction and ORR profiles as the standard 2‐week delay following a dose reduction, and was not expected to provide additional benefit to participants. Discontinuation rates were higher with the 3 mg/kg dose regimens compared to the 4 and 3.5 mg/kg regimens. This can likely be attributed to the more stringent discontinuation requirement, where patients must discontinue treatment following two PN events for the 3 mg/kg regimens, while patients discontinue treatment following three PN events for the 3.5 and 4 mg/kg regimens. Ultimately, simulations predicted the 4 mg/kg starting dose regimen resulted in superior ORR compared to other starting dose regimens after accounting for the more frequent dose modifications due to Grade ≥ 2 PN events. Higher dose modification rates and PN incidence were also predicted for the 4 mg/kg dose. Considering the balance between safety and efficacy in the intended patient population, the simulations suggest 4 mg/kg is the optimal dose. The modeling work presented here was used to evaluate whether PF‐06804103 was a viable candidate to bring forward in development with the changing treatment landscape.

It needs to be acknowledged that the presented analyses had been conducted in a fit‐for‐purpose manner to support dose and program decisions, with areas for further refinement. First, not all AEs that resulted in PF‐06804103 dose modifications (e.g., skin toxicity, myalgia) were incorporated in the simulation. The current work captures Grade ≥ 2 PN, the most frequent AE leading to dose modification. Since a key objective of the modeling work was to inform whether to continue the clinical development of PF‐06804103, the adaptive dosing simulations assumed a best‐case scenario to evaluate whether PF‐06804103 would result in a significant and meaningful improvement in efficacy compared to the changing treatment landscape. As needed, the safety models could certainly be expanded to account for other major AEs leading to dose modifications. Additionally, the key efficacy endpoint evaluated in the adaptive simulations was ORR, but other efficacy endpoints such as duration of response, progression‐free survival, and overall survival were not evaluated due to data limitations at the early stage of development. For investigational agents with sufficient data, additional models may be incorporated into this adaptive dosing framework to predict survival outcomes. Finally, a key consideration for adaptive dosing simulations is that, while they aim to reproduce realistic clinical trials by individualizing treatments for each patient, the simulations assume timely data availability to inform decision making and exact adherence to rule execution. In reality, clinical trials often have missing or noisy data, and clinicians may deviate from the simulation‐assumed rules for practicality or to prioritize patient safety.

In summary, an adaptive dosing simulation framework was established by combining three longitudinal PK and PKPD models to predict safety and efficacy profiles and to support dose optimization of the investigational agent PF‐06804103. This framework provides the advantage of accounting for AE‐driven dose modifications and their real‐time impacts on PK and efficacy, and can be adapted to other oncology therapeutics with time‐dependent and exposure‐related safety and efficacy profiles. The framework could be particularly beneficial to inform dose optimization by integrating multi‐dimensional early clinical data to evaluate different dosage regimens and define the regimen with the best benefit/risk ratio for further investigation.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: Upon request, and subject to certain criteria, conditions, and exceptions (see https://www.pfizer.com/science/clinical‐trials/trial‐data‐and‐results for more information), Pfizer will provide access to individual de‐identified participant data from Pfizer‐sponsored global interventional clinical studies conducted for medicines, vaccines, and medical devices (1) for indications that have been approved in the US and/or EU or (2) in programs that have been terminated (i.e., development for all indications has been discontinued). Pfizer will also consider requests for the protocol, data dictionary, and statistical analysis plan. Data may be requested from Pfizer trials 24 months after study completion. The de‐identified participant data will be made available to researchers whose proposals meet the research criteria and other conditions, and for which an exception does not apply, via a secure portal. To gain access, data requestors must enter into a data access agreement with Pfizer.
